lines.text: A kingdom of a million elephants, a land fought over by its neighbours, and a secret war. This is the story of Laos, along the Mekong.
Some two thousand years ago, people scattered thousands of great stone jars across a high plain. Why, no one knows for sure.
In the thirteen hundreds, a prince named Fa Ngum set out to unite the Lao lands under one crown.
He founded Lan Xang, the land of a million elephants, ruled first from Luang Prabang.
Later its kings moved the capital to Vientiane, on the banks of the Mekong.
There they raised Pha That Luang, a great golden stupa that is still the symbol of the nation.
After Lan Xang split into three kingdoms and fell under Siam, France took control in 1893.
Kaysone Phomvihane was born, the communist who would lead Laos from 1975.
In 1953, Laos became independent, a small landlocked kingdom caught between greater powers.
Soon a civil war began. For sixteen years Laos was bombed more heavily than any country before, until the Pathet Lao took power.
Through its jungles ran the Ho Chi Minh trail, the supply route from North to South Vietnam that drew the bombs.
And in 2021, a new railway opened from the Chinese border to Vientiane, linking Laos to the world beyond.
From the stone jars to a railway of today, Laos endures, quiet, along its river.
